question.text: Under the SEBI Delisting of Equity Shares Regulations, 2021, what type of resolution is required from shareholders for voluntary delisting?

explanation.text: The Logic: Voluntary delisting permanently removes a company's shares from the trading platform of stock exchanges and ends public-investor liquidity, so it is treated as a fundamental corporate action requiring a higher threshold of shareholder consent. Under the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021, the company must obtain approval of its shareholders by way of a special resolution passed through postal ballot or e-voting, where the votes cast by public shareholders in favour must be at least two times the votes cast against (the "2x public shareholder" test). The "special resolution" requirement (passed by at least a 2/3 majority of those voting) is the standard companies-law threshold for such structurally significant decisions. The Trap: An ordinary resolution (simple majority) is reserved for routine business and is too low a bar for permanently removing trading access. A unanimous resolution would make delisting practically impossible and is not what the regulation prescribes. A board resolution without shareholder approval would bypass the very investors whose exit rights are at stake and is therefore inadmissible. Note: The cited workbook pages (44-50 and 226 of the NISM Series IX Merchant Banking workbook) discuss the voluntary delisting process, board approval, public notice, prior shareholder approval, and merchant banker appointment, but they do not explicitly characterise the required shareholder resolution as a "special resolution (2/3 majority)." The framing above reflects the general regulatory/legal position under SEBI's delisting regulations and the Companies Act treatment of special resolutions.
